record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: For decentralized partial-search peer-to-peer systems, does there exist a general search technique that can guarantee, with high probability, that the tradeoff between resource cost and the chosen quality-of-service metric is optimal?

evidence.quote: Can there exist a general technique that can guarantee (with high probability) that the cost/QoS tradeoff is optimal?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a decentralized peer-to-peer system modeled as a dynamic network of nodes, where each node stores a subset of data items and communicates only with a bounded number of neighbors. A partial-search algorithm is a distributed protocol that, given a query for a data item, terminates after locating some (not necessarily all) copies of the item in the network. Associated with such an algorithm are two measures: a resource cost C (e.g., total number of messages exchanged, bandwidth consumed, or nodes visited) and a quality-of-service metric Q (e.g., probability of locating a copy, search latency, or fraction of available copies discovered). For a given workload and network model, a (C, Q) pair is called Pareto-optimal if no algorithm achieves strictly better cost without degrading Q, and vice versa.

Question: Does there exist a general (universal) decentralized partial-search technique that, for every reasonable choice of quality-of-service metric Q and every workload/network instance from a broad class, achieves with high probability a (cost, QoS) tradeoff that is Pareto-optimal?

Either exhibit such a general technique together with a proof of its optimality, or prove that no such universal technique exists.
artifact.status_search_result: No specific resolution of this general question about a universal optimal cost/QoS tradeoff technique for decentralized partial-search peer-to-peer systems was located. The question remains posed as an open challenge with no evidence of a definitive solution.
